system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C cirrhosis and portal hypertension, was admitted for melena and hematemesis following recent esophageal variceal banding. He presented with hypotension and evidence of upper GI bleeding, requiring transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells. An EGD revealed an esophageal ulcer and blood in the stomach, but no active bleeding; the previously placed variceal bands had dislodged. He was treated with octreotide, ceftriaxone (later switched to oral ciprofloxacin), and IV pantoprazole, which was transitioned to oral pantoprazole twice daily. Nadolol was held due to bradycardia, likely related to octreotide, but was restarted at discharge at half dose. His condition stabilized, hemoglobin remained steady, and he tolerated a diet advance. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a course of ciprofloxacin and sucralfate, continue high-dose PPI therapy, and follow up for repeat EGD and hepatology evaluation.
problems: Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, with bleeding
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Other drugs and medicinal substances causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

TACE procedure:
*** UNAPPROVED (PRELIMINARY) REPORT ***
INDICATION: ___ male with multifocal HCC. Transarterial
chemoembolization requested.
 
COMPARISON: MR of ___.
 
PHYSICIANS: Dr. ___ (attending, present and supervising 
throughout)
and Dr. ___ (fellow).
 
ANESTHESIA/MEDICATIONS: Moderate sedation was provided by 
administering
divided doses of fentanyl (75 mcg) and Versed (1.5 mg) 
throughout the total
intraservice time of 1 hour and 35 minutes during which the 
patient's
hemodynamic parameters were monitored continuously by an 
independent radiology
nurse. In addition, the patient received 30 mg IV Toradol, 20 mL
intra-arterial 1% lidocaine and 0.25 mg of Dilaudid. 
Chemoembolization
consisted of 6 mg of doxorubicin and 20 mL of lipiodol.
 
FLUOROSCOPY: 655 mGy, 29 minutes.
 
CONTRAST: 108 mL Optiray.
 
PROCEDURES:
1. Right CFA access with a micropuncture needle.
2. Common hepatic arteriogram and rotational cone-beam CT.
3. Transarterial chemoembolization of the right hepatic artery
 
PROCEDURE DETAIL: After explanation of the risks, benefits and 
alternatives
to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained. The 
patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the 
imaging table. The
right groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. 
A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ 
protocol.
 
Under palpatory, ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance, the right 
common
femoral artery was accessed with a micropuncture needle. A 0.018 
nitinol wire
was then advanced through the needle into the lower abdominal 
aorta. A small
skin incision was made over the needle and the needle was 
exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath. The inner cannula and dilator were removed 
with the
wire and a 0.035 ___ wire was advanced through the 
micropuncture sheath
into the lower abdominal aorta. The sheath was removed and a 5 
___
___ sheath was advanced over the wire. The sheath was then 
connected to
a continuous heparinized side arm flush.
 
Next, a C2 glide catheter was advanced over the ___ wire 
into the upper
abdominal aorta. The wire was removed and the celiac axis was 
selectively
cannulated, confirmed by a hand injection of contrast. With the 
assistance of
a Glidewire, the catheter was then advanced more distally into 
the common
hepatic artery. Digital subtraction angiogram with rotational 
DynaCT was
performed demonstrating conventional hepatic arterial anatomy. 
There are
several abnormal vessels arising from the proximal aspect of the 
right hepatic
artery supplying subtle areas of tumoral enhancement 
corresponding to findings
on MRI. The C2 catheter was advanced into the right hepatic 
artery and
chemoembolization was administered with tumor staining, 
particularly in the
segment VI/VII lesion. Next, a small amount Gelfoam was 
administered for
bland embolization to slow vascular flow. The patient received 5 
mL aliquots
of intra-arterial 1% lidocaine intermittently between 
administration of the
chemoembolization. The catheter was flushed and removed. The 
sheath was
removed and hemostasis was achieved with 15 minutes of manual 
compression.
 
The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate 
complication.
 
FINDINGS:
1. Conventional common hepatic arterial anatomy with multiple 
branches
arising from the right common hepatic artery and supplying the 
dominant tumor
as well as smaller tumors.
2. Slowed flow to the dominant lesion and other lesions after 
administration
of chemoembolization and bland embolization material.
 
IMPRESSION: Uncomplicated transarterial chemoembolization to the 
RHA.
Findings and recommendations discussed with Dr. ___ at 1 
p.m. on
___.

CT abdomen post TACE
TECHNIQUE:  CT of the abdomen without IV contrast.
 
FINDINGS:  Lung bases are clear.  There is no Lipiodol 
distribution in the
lung bases.
 
ABDOMEN:  Within the liver, the dominant tumor in segment VI/VII 
has dense
Lipiodol uptake as does the remainder of the right lobe of the 
liver.  Air
noted within the liver (3, 17 and 3, 26), likely a result of 
recent
procedure.There is no non-targeted Lipiodol uptake noted.  The 
gallbladder
contains dense stones.
 
Non-contrast appearance of the pancreas and stomach are 
unremarkable.  The
spleen is enlarged at 18 cm.  The renal vasculature contain 
scattered
calcifications as does the abdominal aorta.  There are also tiny 
punctate
calcifications in bilateral kidneys representing very small 
stones,
non-obstructing.  A renal cyst is noted all through the right 
kidney.
 
The mesentery is in general misty with a small amount of fluid, 
likely ascites
in both paracolic gutters.  There is a recanalized umbilical 
vein along with
prominent varices elsewhere throughout the abdomen including 
gastric and
esophageal.  
 
IMPRESSION:
1.  Good Lipiodol uptake within the dominant liver lesion as 
well as in the
remainder of the right lobe of the liver.  No non-target 
embolization
identified.
2.  Splenomegaly, varices, tiny renal non-obstructing renal 
stones and
cholelithiasis.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with multifocal HCC.  Transarterial
chemoembolization requested.

COMPARISON:  MR of ___.

PHYSICIANS: Dr. ___ (attending, present and supervising throughout)
and Dr. ___ (fellow).

ANESTHESIA/MEDICATIONS:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering
divided doses of fentanyl (75 mcg) and Versed (1.5 mg) throughout the total
intraservice time of 1 hour and 35 minutes during which the patient's
hemodynamic parameters were monitored continuously by an independent radiology
nurse.  In addition, the patient received 30 mg IV Toradol, 20 mL
intra-arterial 1% lidocaine and 0.25 mg of Dilaudid.  Chemoembolization
consisted of 6 mg of doxorubicin and 20 mL of lipiodol.

FLUOROSCOPY:  655 mGy, 29 minutes.

CONTRAST:  108 mL Optiray.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Right CFA access with a micropuncture needle.
2.  Common hepatic arteriogram and rotational cone-beam CT.
3.  Transarterial chemoembolization of the right hepatic artery 

PROCEDURE DETAIL:  After explanation of the risks, benefits and alternatives
to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The
right groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ protocol.

Under palpatory, ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance, the right common
femoral artery was accessed with a micropuncture needle.  A 0.018 nitinol wire
was then advanced through the needle into the lower abdominal aorta.  A small
skin incision was made over the needle and the needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath.  The inner cannula and dilator were removed with the
wire and a 0.035 ___ wire was advanced through the micropuncture sheath
into the lower abdominal aorta.  The sheath was removed and a 5 ___
___ sheath was advanced over the wire.  The sheath was then connected to
a continuous heparinized side arm flush.  

Next, a C2 glide catheter was advanced over the ___ wire into the upper
abdominal aorta.  The wire was removed and the celiac axis was selectively
cannulated, confirmed by a hand injection of contrast.  With the assistance of
a Glidewire, the catheter was then advanced more distally into the common
hepatic artery.  Digital subtraction angiogram with rotational DynaCT was
performed demonstrating conventional hepatic arterial anatomy.  There are
several abnormal vessels arising from the proximal aspect of the right hepatic
artery supplying subtle areas of tumoral enhancement corresponding to findings
on MRI.  The C2 catheter was advanced into the right hepatic artery and
chemoembolization was administered with tumor staining, particularly in the
segment VI/VII lesion.  Next, a small amount Gelfoam was administered for
bland embolization to slow vascular flow.  The patient received 5 mL aliquots
of intra-arterial 1% lidocaine intermittently between administration of the
chemoembolization.  The catheter was flushed and removed.  The sheath was
removed and hemostasis was achieved with 15 minutes of manual compression.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complication.

Of note, the 3D CT was performed (including multiplanar reformatted images)
was performed on an independent workstation.

FINDINGS:
1.  Cone beam CT demonstrates conventional common hepatic arterial anatomy
with multiple branches arising from the right common hepatic artery and
supplying the dominant tumor as well as smaller tumors.
2.  Slowed flow to the dominant lesion and other lesions after administration
of chemoembolization and bland embolization material.

___.

lung bases.

ABDOMEN:  Within the liver, the dominant tumor in segment VI/VII has dense
Lipiodol uptake as does the remainder of the right lobe of the liver.  Air
noted within the liver (3, 17 and 3, 26), likely a result of recent
procedure.There is no non-targeted Lipiodol uptake noted.  The gallbladder
contains dense stones.

Non-contrast appearance of the pancreas and stomach are unremarkable.  The

calcifications as does the abdominal aorta.  There are also tiny punctate
calcifications in bilateral kidneys representing very small stones,

The mesentery is in general misty with a small amount of fluid, likely ascites
in both paracolic gutters.  There is a recanalized umbilical vein along with
prominent varices elsewhere throughout the abdomen including gastric and
esophageal.  

IMPRESSION:
1.  Good Lipiodol uptake within the dominant liver lesion as well as in the
remainder of the right lobe of the liver.  No non-target embolization

2.  Splenomegaly, varices, tiny renal non-obstructing renal stones and
cholelithiasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You’ve just come back from the procedure suite after your TACE treatment. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m okay. A little groggy, but no pain or anything. They said it went well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the procedure went very smoothly. You had a transarterial chemoembolization, or TACE, which means they delivered chemotherapy directly into the liver tumor through its blood supply and then blocked the vessel to keep the drug there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, that’s what they explained. The big tumor in segment six and seven, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The radiologist confirmed the anatomy and delivered the chemo—doxorubicin mixed with a special oil called lipiodol—right into the artery feeding that 5.2 cm tumor. They also treated two smaller ones in segment eight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no damage to the rest of the liver? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. The goal is to target only the tumor. The report says there was no non-target embolization, meaning the chemo stayed where it was supposed to. Your healthy liver tissue should be spared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about side effects? They said I might feel sick later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients develop what we call post-embolization syndrome—fever, mild nausea, or fatigue over the next few days. But you’re not having nausea now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not right now. Just a little tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll monitor you closely. You’ll stay overnight for observation. We’ll check your liver enzymes tomorrow with a blood test and a CT scan to confirm the lipiodol is where it should be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my regular meds? I take a lot for my liver and heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve reviewed them. You’re on nadolol for portal hypertension, furosemide and spironolactone for fluid, omeprazole for stomach protection, and others. We’ll restart those tomorrow morning unless there’s a reason not to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was in, they held my nadolol because my heart rate dropped. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch your heart rate closely. Right now it’s 57, which is stable. We’ll only restart the nadolol if it stays in a safe range. Your ECG today was normal, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes meds? Glyburide twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that. Your blood sugar this morning was 159, which is acceptable. We’ll check it again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. One more thing—my last MRI mentioned cysts in the pancreas. Did they say anything about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the MRI did show multiple cysts in the head of the pancreas, possibly IPMNs. That’s not related to the liver cancer, but we recommend follow-up imaging later to monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to ask my doctor about that later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your CT scan from this morning. It shows excellent uptake of the lipiodol in the tumor and the right lobe of the liver. No spread to other areas, including the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. So the treatment hit the target?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The radiologist confirmed no non-target embolization. There’s some expected air in the liver from the procedure, but that’s harmless and will resolve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver numbers? I know they usually go up after this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your AST and ALT are elevated—222 and 157—but that’s expected after TACE. It means the liver cells are reacting to the treatment. They should come down in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No sign of infection or bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your white blood cell count is normal, and the CT shows no bleeding or fluid collections. Your groin site is healing well, and you’ve had no fever so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a little warm last night, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be the start of post-embolization fever. It’s common. We’ll give you acetaminophen if it comes back. Just let the nurse know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another TACE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That will be decided at the tumor board. This was your first session. Depending on how this tumor responds, they may recommend another in a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cirrhosis? Does this affect my overall liver function?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver function is still compensated. Bilirubin and creatinine are normal. As long as you don’t develop complications like ascites or confusion, you’re in a good position to tolerate further treatments if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have the varices. Should I watch for bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that risk remains due to portal hypertension. That’s why you’re on nadolol and omeprazole. Keep taking them as prescribed. Report any black stools or vomiting blood immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So, am I going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this afternoon. You’ve done well—no nausea, pain, or complications. You’ll go home with some medications for nausea and pain, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Prochlorperazine for nausea, acetaminophen and a small amount of oxycodone for pain if needed. And we’re adding ranitidine for extra stomach protection for the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please get your blood work—basic metabolic panel and liver tests—done in about a week. Fax the results to Dr. ___’s office so we can monitor your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for a few days. No heavy lifting for a week. Walk around to stay active, but listen to your body. Fever is expected, but if it goes above 101 or you feel worse, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a follow-up with your oncologist and hepatologist in two weeks. They’ll review the imaging and decide on next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I appreciate the time you took to explain everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Just take care of yourself, take your meds, and we’ll see how you’re doing at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set, Mr. ___. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Take meds, check labs, follow up in two weeks, call if I feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for post-procedural observation after undergoing transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) of a 5.2 cm liver tumor in segment VI/VII and smaller lesions in segment VIII. The procedure was uncomplicated, with successful delivery of doxorubicin-lipiodol and no non-target embolization. He remained stable throughout admission, with no significant pain, nausea, or complications. Post-procedure CT confirmed good lipiodol uptake in the target lesions and no ectopic distribution. Liver enzymes rose modestly as expected. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to monitor for post-embolization symptoms, complete outpatient lab testing, and follow up with oncology and hepatology. All home medications, including nadolol, diuretics, and omeprazole, were continued.
